beats.text: American flight schools wouldn't teach her. So she learned French.

overlays.hook: American flight schools wouldn't teach her. So she learned *French.*

beats.text: Born in Texas in 1892, she was one of thirteen children.
She was working as a manicurist in Chicago when she decided to fly.
Flight schools there turned her down, because she was Black and a woman.
So she learned French and sailed to France.

visual.caption: The flying school at Le Crotoy, France, 1916

beats.text: At the Caudron brothers' school, she trained in fragile biplanes,

visual.caption: A Caudron G.3, the kind of biplane French schools trained on

beats.text: and on June 15, 1921, she earned her pilot's license,

visual.caption: Her license from the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale

beats.text: the first African American woman ever to do it.

visual.caption: Bessie Coleman in her flying helmet

beats.text: Back home, she flew loops and figure eights at air shows.
In Jim Crow America, she pushed back against segregated audiences.
A crash in 1923 broke her leg. She healed, and flew again.

visual.sub: a broken leg, and back in the air

beats.text: In 1926, she died in a crash while rehearsing for an air show.
She never got to open her flight school for Black pilots. But she opened the sky.
Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

facts.claim: US flight schools would not train her, so she learned French (to apply to French schools).
Born in Texas in 1892, one of 13 children.
facts.note: Town differs: NWHM says Waxahachie; other sources Atlanta, Texas (also on her licence). The script says only 'Texas'. Her licence gives 1896 as birth year; historians give 1892.

facts.claim: Worked as a manicurist in Chicago before learning to fly.
US flight schools rejected her because she was Black and a woman.
facts.note: NASM: getting a licence in the US 'proved impossible' for an African American woman.

facts.claim: Learned French and sailed to France (November 1920).
Trained at the Caudron brothers' school at Le Crotoy.
Licence from the FAI dated 15 June 1921.
First African American woman to earn a pilot's licence.
facts.note: NWHM also calls her the first American of any race or gender awarded the FAI licence directly; that wider claim is not used.

facts.claim: Stunt flying: loops and figure eights at air shows.
Refused / resisted segregated crowds at her shows.
facts.note: NASM: 'would only perform in exhibition shows if the crowds were desegregated'. NWHM gives a case (Waxahachie) where she demanded one entrance and had to accept a compromise. Script says 'pushed back against', which both support.

facts.claim: 1923 crash in California, broken leg; she recovered and flew again.
Died 30 April 1926 in a crash while rehearsing for an air show.
facts.note: Place (Jacksonville, Florida) not used on screen.

facts.claim: She never opened the flight school for Black pilots she was saving for.
facts.note: 'She opened the sky' is a closing line, not a factual claim.
